newsitem.title: USA: World Bank chief to urge attack on corruption.
newsitem.headline: World Bank chief to urge attack on corruption.

text.p: By Rich Miller, U.S. Economics Correspondent
World Bank President James Wolfensohn was set to admonish developing nations on Tuesday about bribery and corruption and offer his organisation's help in a drive to stamp out the problems.

Bank officials said the plain-speaking Wolfensohn intended to use part of his opening speech to the plenary session of the Bank and the International Monetary Fund to throw a spotlight on a problem often hidden out of sight in the past.
Wolfensohn is concerned that corruption undercuts the effectiveness of the billions of dolars in loans the Bank hands out each year to developing countries.
It also threatens to rob the Bank of support in industrial countries as governments -- and the voters who elect them -- wonder if the money they have contributed is being squandered.

"It has become increasingly clear that bribery and corruption undermine good governance and the effective use of scarce aid resources," U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin told the joint Development Committee of the Bank and the IMF.
He called on the World Bank and regional development banks on Monday to do more to tackle the problem.

"We urge all of the multilateral development banks to work collaboratively to establish uniform rules, to require use of standard bidding documents, and to have strong headquarters oversight of the procurement process," Rubin said on Monday.

Wolfensohn and the World Bank are already taking action against corruption. The organisation's board recently set new procurement guidelines for projects financed by its loans -- action which Rubin applauded.

Under the new guidelines, the Bank can cancel part of a loan if it determines that corrupt or fraudulent practices were involved in procurement contracts. It can also bar guilty companies from bidding on future bank-financed projects.
"The Bank is undertaking a renewed approach to helping countries prevent corruption," the organisation said in a fact sheet on the issue.

The World Bank said that economic and other reforms in developing countries, including stronger regulation of monopolies, better pay for civil servants and tough government procurement practices, can help the battle against bribery.

The IMF has also taken a look at the problem. Asked at news conference about corruption in Argentina, IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus said, "Corruption (is) one of the problems which is a serious one for Argentina, as its is for so many countries in the world."

Chilean Finance Minister Eduardo Aninat, who is acting as chairman of the IMF/World Bank annual meeting, told reporters that if corruption was rubbed out in developing countries, more money would be freed up for social programmes.
"We have to make sure that of every dollar spent on social programmes, most of it makes it to the people who need it," he said Monday.
